transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Reykjavik, Iceland at 2026-04-14 12:21 GMT (UTC+0000) (2026-04-14T12:21:00Z in UTC), at latitude 64.1466 degrees and longitude -21.9426 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 34.122 degrees and its azimuth is 159.921 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 18.176 degrees and its azimuth is 200.971 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 11.39 percent illuminated, 39.356 degrees from the Sun, and 375827.9 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably not with the unaided eye—though it is not strictly impossible.

The Moon is geometrically well above the horizon at **18.2°**, but it is only an **11.4%-illuminated waning crescent**, just **39.4° from the Sun**. In bright daylight, that thin crescent has low contrast against the blue sky. Its relatively low altitude also adds atmospheric haze and scattering.

For an ordinary observer who only roughly knows where to look, I would rate unaided-eye detection as **unlikely**. Exceptionally transparent Icelandic air and using a building to block the Sun might make it possible, especially with an exact positional reference. **Binoculars should make it much easier**, but only if the Sun is securely hidden behind a solid object—never sweep binoculars anywhere near the visible Sun.

So: **above the horizon, yes; realistically naked-eye visible right then, probably not.**
